1: Paul blesses God, who comforts us in every trouble so that we can comfort others. He describes a danger in Asia so severe that he despaired of life, and explains why he changed his plans to visit.
Suffering shared with Christ equips us to console others. God's promises all find their "Yes" in Jesus.
2: Paul wrote an earlier letter in tears. Now he urges the Corinthians to forgive and comfort someone who has been punished enough. Christians are "the aroma of Christ" wherever they go.
Church discipline aims at restoring people. Once someone repents, mercy should be quick.
3: The Corinthians themselves are Paul's letter of recommendation, written by the Spirit on hearts. The old covenant on stone had glory; the new covenant of the Spirit has far more. With unveiled faces we are being changed into the Lord's likeness.
"The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." The Christian life is a gradual transformation.
4: Paul does not lose heart. The light of the Gospel is carried in fragile human beings, so that the power is clearly God's. Afflicted but not crushed, he looks to what is unseen and eternal.
God works through weak people on purpose. Present troubles are light compared with the glory to come.
5: Our earthly body is a tent; God is preparing an eternal home. We walk by faith, not by sight, and all must appear before Christ's judgement seat. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God has given the apostles the ministry of reconciliation.
"Be reconciled to God." The Church sees the ministry of reconciliation continued in the sacrament of confession.
6: Now is the day of salvation

Paul lists the hardships that prove his ministry: beatings, sleepless nights, hunger, yet always rejoicing. He urges the Corinthians to open their hearts and not to be yoked together with unbelievers.
Do not put off responding to grace. Close partnerships shape who we become.
7: Titus brings news that the Corinthians took Paul's severe letter well. Paul rejoices: sorrow that leads to repentance brings salvation and no regret, while worldly sorrow only produces death.
There are two kinds of feeling bad about sin. The good kind moves us to change.
8: The poor churches of Macedonia gave beyond their means for the Christians in Jerusalem. Paul encourages Corinth to finish its own collection, pointing to Christ, who was rich and became poor for our sake.
Christian giving imitates Jesus. The aim is that those with plenty supply those in need.
9: Whoever sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under pressure. God is able to provide all that is needed for every good work.
Generosity is an act of trust in God, and it produces thanksgiving to him.
10: Critics say Paul is bold in letters but unimpressive in person. He answers that his weapons are spiritual, able to demolish arguments, and that he boasts only in the Lord.
The battle for souls is fought with truth, not worldly methods. We take every thought captive to obey Christ.
11: False apostles are impressing the Corinthians. Paul reluctantly lists what he has suffered: five floggings, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, hunger, cold, and daily anxiety for the churches.
The marks of a true apostle are sufferings borne for Christ, not polish or success.
12: Paul speaks of being caught up to paradise. To keep him humble he was given "a thorn in the flesh". Three times he begged the Lord to remove it and was told, "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness."
God sometimes leaves a weakness in place and gives the grace to bear it. "When I am weak, then I am strong."
13: Paul warns that on his third visit he will not spare those who keep sinning. He tells the Corinthians to test whether they are living in the faith, and closes with a blessing that names Christ, God and the Holy Spirit.
The final blessing is used as a greeting at Mass. Self-examination is a normal part of Christian life.
